n: Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and then go speak to Israel. Before he can teach God’s word, he must take it fully into himself.
Ezekiel obeys—unlike the rebellious house—and God feeds him the scroll.

f.g: God himself provides what the prophet needs.

n: Surprisingly, a scroll full of woe tastes sweet as honey. Doing God’s will and receiving his word brings sweetness, even when the message is hard.
Now he must go and speak God’s words—not his own—to Israel.
Ezekiel is not being sent to foreigners whose language he can’t understand, but to his own people.
Ironically, if God had sent him to foreign nations, they would have listened. Jesus made a similar point about Gentiles who repented more readily than his own people.

f.w: they would have hearkened unto thee

n: Israel won’t listen to Ezekiel because they won’t listen to God himself. Their rejection is not personal.

f.w: they will not hearken unto me

n: God makes Ezekiel’s face and forehead as hard as theirs. His name, which means “God strengthens” or “God hardens,” fits this promise.

f.g: A play on the name Ezekiel (Yeḥezqel, “God makes strong”).

n: His forehead will be harder than flint. He will be able to stand firm against stubborn hearers.

f.g: The hardest stone—perhaps emery or diamond.

n: Before speaking, Ezekiel must take God’s words into his heart and listen carefully. Inner reception precedes outward preaching.
His specific mission is to the exiles—his own people in captivity—whether they listen or not.

f.g: The Jewish exiles deported to Babylon in 597 BC.

n: The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up, and he hears a great rushing sound behind him praising the glory of the LORD.

f.w: Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place
f.g: Some scholars suggest a small text change reading “as the glory of the LORD rose from its place.”

n: The rushing comes from the creatures’ wings and the wheels as the chariot-throne departs.
Ezekiel goes away bitter and agitated—perhaps sharing God’s indignation at Israel’s sin, or overwhelmed by his assignment—but God’s hand is strongly upon him.

f.w: in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit

n: At Tel-abib, the exiles’ settlement, Ezekiel sits among them stunned for seven days—the traditional length of mourning, and the length of a priest’s ordination.

f.g: “Mound of the flood” or “of spring”; a settlement of Jewish exiles by the Chebar canal (modern Tel Aviv took its name from this verse).

n: After seven days God speaks to him again.

f.w: at the end of seven days
f.g: A new stage of his commission follows his silent week.

n: God makes Ezekiel a watchman. Like a sentry on a city wall who warns of approaching danger, a prophet must sound the alarm about spiritual danger.
If Ezekiel fails to warn the wicked, they will still die for their sins, but God will hold Ezekiel responsible. Leaders are accountable for warning those in their care.

f.w: his blood will I require at thine hand

n: If he warns them and they ignore him, they bear their own guilt, and Ezekiel has saved his own soul.
The duty applies to the righteous too. If a good person turns to sin and the watchman stays silent, both answer for it. Past righteousness does not cancel present wickedness.

f.g: An obstacle or test that reveals a person’s choices.

f.w: his righteousness which he hath done shall not be remembered

n: But if the watchman warns a righteous person and they heed it, they will live—and the watchman is also saved. Warning is an act of love.

f.w: he shall surely live, because he is warned

n: God’s hand rests on Ezekiel again, and he is told to go out to the plain for further instruction.

f.g: A valley or open plain near Tel-abib.

n: There he sees the same glory he saw by the Chebar and falls on his face once more.
The Spirit raises him again and tells him to shut himself in his house—his ministry will begin with dramatic silence.

f.g: His home became the place where elders came to consult him.

n: Ezekiel will be bound with ropes and unable to go out among the people—whether literally restrained by others or held back by God.
God will make him unable to speak except when giving God’s word. This silence lasted until news of Jerusalem’s fall reached the exiles years later.

f.w: I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth

n: When God has a message, he will open Ezekiel’s mouth. Then the choice is the people’s: whoever will hear, let him hear. Jesus used similar words.

f.w: He that heareth, let him hear
